beats.intro: Module two. [[sub]]Same bond, different cash flow shapes. And the options that can change them.
beats.bullet: The standard bond is the bullet bond. [[a]]The investor lends three hundred million. [[b]]The issuer pays only interest, four point eight million every six months. [[c]]All the principal comes back in one bullet, at maturity. [[d]]Governments and companies use it most, and investors like the known income and the set maturity.
beats.amort: Now the opposite: a fully amortizing loan. [[f]]The same three hundred million, the same three point two percent, the same five years. The level payment is the rate times principal, divided by one minus one plus the rate, to the power of minus N. That comes to thirty two point seven million every six months. [[bars]]Each payment is interest plus principal. [[int]]Interest is charged on the balance still owed, so it shrinks over time. [[prin]]Principal grows to fill the gap. [[end]]By the last payment, the balance is zero. Mortgages work this way.
beats.balloon: A partially amortizing bond sits in between. [[a]]It pays down part of the principal over time, and leaves a balloon payment of one hundred fifty million at maturity. Here is how much principal is still owed, under each structure. [[b]]The bullet bond owes the full amount until the very end. [[c]]The fully amortizing loan owes less and less, until nothing. [[d]]Amortizing gives investors higher early cash flow and lower credit risk, because the amount owed shrinks. But it brings reinvestment risk, because rates may fall before the cash is reinvested.
beats.sinking: Two more ways to retire principal early. [[sink]]A sinking fund. The issuer sets money aside, and retires part of the bond before maturity, for example by redeeming randomly chosen bonds. [[wf]]And a waterfall, used in asset-backed securities. Everyone gets interest, but principal is paid in order. Tranche A first. Tranche B only after A is fully repaid. Then tranche C. [[end]]Losses hit the junior tranche first. Both structures reduce credit risk, and both add reinvestment risk.
beats.variable: Now variable interest debt. [[f]]A floating-rate note pays a market reference rate, plus a credit spread. [[ex]]Take a note with a spread of two point five percent. When the reference rate is minus half a percent, the coupon is two percent. [[b]]When the reference rate rises to point one five percent, the coupon becomes two point six five. [[c]]At point two five, two point seven five. [[d]]At half a percent, three percent. [[e]]On two hundred fifty million euros, paid quarterly, the interest payments are one point two five million, one point six five six million, one point seven one nine million, and one point eight seven five million. [[risk]]Because the coupon adjusts, there is less interest rate risk. But credit risk remains.
beats.special: Coupons can also adjust in other ways. [[step]]A step-up bond raises its coupon by a set margin on set dates. [[credit]]A credit-linked coupon rises if the issuer's credit weakens, for example when its leverage ratio grows. [[pik]]A payment-in-kind feature pays interest by adding to the principal instead of paying cash. It helps issuers who are short of cash, and usually comes with a higher rate. [[esg]]Even strong issuers use these designs. A sustainability-linked bond may add fifty basis points if the issuer misses a carbon target.
beats.indexed: Index-linked bonds tie payments to an index, most often inflation. [[tips]]In a capital-indexed bond, the principal is adjusted. Say an investor holds one hundred fifteen million of inflation-protected bonds, with a one percent coupon. [[cpi]]The price index rises from two sixty five to two sixty seven point two five. That is up point eight four nine percent. [[adj]]The principal becomes one hundred fifteen point nine seven six million. [[coup]]One percent of that, split in two, gives a half-year coupon of five hundred seventy nine thousand, eight hundred eighty two dollars. [[int]]In an interest-indexed bond, only the coupon adjusts, and the principal stays fixed.
beats.zero: Zero-coupon bonds pay nothing until maturity. [[a]]They are sold at a discount to par, and the difference is the investor's interest. [[b]]They suit a fixed future obligation, because there are no coupons to reinvest. [[c]]A deferred coupon bond pays nothing for the first few years, then a higher coupon. Issuers use it to conserve cash, and it is also priced at a discount.
beats.calls: Now the contingency provisions, which can change the cash flows. [[call]]A callable bond lets the issuer redeem before maturity. [[prot]]There is usually a call protection period, when the bond cannot be called. Then a schedule of call prices. For a seven year note, no call for three years, then one hundred three point two five, then one hundred two point five, and so on down. [[cap]]The call price caps how high the bond's price can rise when yields fall. When yields are above the coupon, the issuer has no reason to call, and the bond behaves like a normal one. [[comp]]Because investors take call risk, a callable bond yields more than a similar non-callable bond. [[make]]A make-whole call pays a high price, based on a government yield, so it is rarely used.
beats.puts: A putable bond lets the investor sell it back to the issuer, usually at par. [[a]]If yields rise and the price falls, the investor can put the bond, and reinvest at the higher rates. [[b]]So the put price acts as a floor under the bond's price. [[c]]The investor owns this option, so the bond costs more, and yields less, than a similar bond with no put.
beats.convert: A convertible bond can be exchanged for shares. [[ex]]Take a bond with a face value of one thousand euros, and a conversion price of forty two. [[ratio]]The conversion ratio is one thousand divided by forty two, which is twenty three point eight one shares. [[prem]]With the shares at twenty eight euros, that conversion price is a fifty percent premium. [[val]]Later, the shares trade at thirty five. The conversion value is twenty three point eight one times thirty five, which is eight hundred thirty three euros and thirty five cents. [[hold]]That is below the bond's price of one thousand, so the investor keeps the bond. [[up]]If the shares soar well above the conversion price, the bond's price tracks its conversion value. [[low]]If the shares stay low, it behaves like an ordinary bond. [[coco]]A contingent convertible, or CoCo, works on the downside. It converts automatically, for instance when a bank's capital falls below its minimum, so it pays a higher yield.
beats.markets: Where a bond is issued matters. [[dom]]A domestic bond is issued by a local company, in its own country. [[for]]A foreign bond is issued by a foreign borrower, in the local market. [[euro]]A Eurobond is issued outside any single country's jurisdiction, in any currency, with lighter regulation. [[glob]]A global bond is issued in the Eurobond market and in at least one domestic market at once. [[note]]But the currency matters more for the price than the place of issue. [[sukuk]]And sukuk replace interest with a share of the returns of real assets, to follow Islamic law.
beats.tax: Taxes also shape returns. [[int]]Interest is usually taxed as ordinary income. [[gain]]A gain from selling above the purchase price is a capital gain, often taxed at a different rate, and sometimes lower if held long. [[exempt]]Some government bonds get special treatment. In the United States, Treasury interest is exempt from state tax, and municipal bonds are often exempt from federal tax. [[issuer]]For issuers, interest is usually tax deductible, which is one reason debt can be cheaper than equity. [[oid]]And in many places, the discount on a bond sold below par is treated as interest, taxed as it accrues.
beats.wrap: Let's recap. [[w1]]Bullet, amortizing, floating, zero and deferred coupons are the main cash flow shapes. [[w2]]Amortizing and floating structures reduce credit risk or interest rate risk, but add reinvestment risk. [[w3]]Call options help issuers, and put and conversion options help investors, and each is paid for in yield. [[w4]]Where a bond is issued, and how it is taxed, also affect its cash flows.
